summary: Documents how DNS-based blacklists and whitelists work: lists of IP addresses or domains, mostly used to fight spam, that are distributed and queried through the DNS. It describes the structure of these lists and the query protocol. It is informational, recording existing practice.

eli5.summary: A club keeps a list of troublemakers that you can look up by phone, so doormen everywhere can quickly check whether to let someone in.

questions: how to check if an ip is blacklisted
subtitle: Shared DNS lookups to check if an IP or domain is listed as a blacklist or whitelist entry.

tldr.problem: Email providers and other services need to quickly check if an IP address or domain is known to send spam, malware, or other unwanted traffic.
tldr.mechanism: DNS Blacklists (DNSBLs) and Whitelists (DNSWLs) are lists of IP addresses or domains published as DNS zones. They can be queried through standard DNS lookups to check membership in seconds.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can share reputation lists and check them at scale without needing to download and maintain entire databases locally. This became the de facto standard for distributed spam filtering.

today: RFC 5782 is an Informational standards-track document that remains current. DNSBLs and DNSWLs are still the standard method for distributing reputation lists in email and other services.

sections.title: What Are DNS Blacklists and Whitelists
sections.content:
In 1997, Internet engineers Dave Rand and Paul Vixie started keeping a list of IP addresses that sent them spam. They distributed it as a Real-time Blackhole List (RBL) using BGP routing feeds. Other network operators wanted to block spam at their mail servers but did not want to use BGP. Rand and Vixie then created a DNS-based distribution method that became far more popular. Today, these lists are simply called DNS Blacklists (DNSBLs) or DNS Whitelists (DNSWLs), collectively known as DNSxLs. A DNSBL lists IP addresses or domains believed to send spam or carry malware; a DNSWL lists senders known to be legitimate.

The DNS method works because mail servers already have DNS resolvers and can query these lists instantly without extra software or network connections. The RFC documents how these lists are structured and queried so that different operators can create lists that work the same way.
sections.eli5: A DNSBL is like a phone directory of bad actors. Instead of calling, you send a quick DNS question to check if someone is on the list.

sections.title: How DNSxLs Are Structured
sections.content:
A DNSxL is a zone in the DNS with a specific structure. For an IPv4 address DNSBL called bad.example.com, if the address 192.0.2.99 is listed, you create a DNS entry by reversing the address octets and appending the DNSBL domain: 99.2.0.192.bad.example.com. This entry must have an A record. The A record value is not actually used as an IP address but as a code. The convention is to return 127.0.0.2, though other values in the 127.0.0.0/8 range can mean different things (for example, 127.0.0.4 could flag a different reason for listing). A TXT record can explain why the address is listed, such as "open relay" or "spammy ISP dialup."

For IPv6 addresses, the method is the same but uses all 32 nibbles (hex digits) of the address in reverse order. A DNSBL can also list domain names rather than IP addresses; these entries simply place the domain before the DNSBL domain (for example, bad-site.com.doms.example.net to list the domain bad-site.com).

When an address is listed in multiple categories, the DNSBL can return multiple A records with different values, or use bit masks in a single A record to signal multiple sublists.
sections.eli5: To look up an IP, flip it backwards, add the list's domain, and ask DNS. It answers with a code that tells you what kind of bad actor it is.

sections.title: How Mail Servers Use DNSxLs
sections.content:
A mail server receives an incoming SMTP connection from another mail server. It extracts the sender's IP address and queries the DNSBL by sending a DNS lookup for the reversed address at the DNSBL's domain. If the DNS lookup returns an A record, the address is listed. If it returns NXDOMAIN (no such domain), the address is not listed. Many mail servers check multiple DNSBLs on every incoming connection. A typical workflow checks a list of DNSBLs in turn until it finds a match: if a DNSBL entry exists, the connection is rejected; if a DNSWL entry is found, the connection is accepted; if no match on any list, the connection is accepted.

Alternatively, mail servers or spam filters can use DNSBL entries as inputs to a scoring system where each DNSBL hit adds weight to a spam score. DNSxLs can also be checked after a message arrives by extracting IP addresses from the message's "Received:" headers or from URLs in the message body.

A mail server can use its normal DNS cache to avoid repeated lookups and to speed up retests, or it can cache DNSxL data internally as long as it respects the DNS Time-to-Live (TTL) values.
sections.eli5: When mail arrives, check the sender's IP against the blacklist with one DNS question. If it matches, reject the mail. If it hits the whitelist, accept it.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
A system manager using a DNSBL trusts that the DNSBL operator's management policies are consistent with their own. Poorly chosen DNSBLs can block legitimate mail. A DNSBL's policies can change over time; some operators have shut down their DNSBLs by removing all entries or installing a wildcard that matches everything.

Because A records in a DNSxL zone represent list entries rather than actual IP addresses, a client that mistakenly uses these entries as real IP addresses (for example, trying to browse 99.2.0.192.bad.example.com as a web server) will get unexpected results. To defend against abandoned DNSBLs that have been re-registered with new, misleading content, clients should check the DNSBL's test entries (every DNSxL MUST contain an entry for test address 127.0.0.2 and MUST NOT contain one for 127.0.0.1) to verify the domain is actually a valid DNSxL.

DNSxLs are subject to standard DNS attacks like spoofing, denial of service, and cache poisoning. Since DNSBL queries happen for nearly every incoming email, DNSBL operators can extract approximate mail volume statistics from DNS server logs.
sections.eli5: Trust the list operator to be fair, or you might block good mail. Bad lists could cause problems, so check test entries to make sure a list is real.
